newsitem.title: UK: Energy consumers slam controversial EU tax plan.
newsitem.headline: Energy consumers slam controversial EU tax plan.

text.p: A European Commission plan to raise minimum taxes on motor and heating fuels and extend their scope to electricity and natural gas threatens jobs and investments, leading industrial energy consumers said on Friday.

The International Federation of Industrial Energy Consumers (IFIEC), whose members represent 75-80 percent of industrial energy consumption in Europe, said the tax would put an unfair burden on industrial processes without taking into account the economic or competitive state of specific industries.

"The tax proposal would substantially reduce company cash flow, with inevitable effects on investment and employment," the IFIEC said in a statement. "Such a tax would also reduce the ability of companies to undertake energy efficiency investments."
The EU Commission agreed a controversial draft law on Wednesday to raise the minimum taxes on motor and heating fuels and to extend taxes to electricity and natural gas.
EU finance ministers will have the final word on the draft law which industry bodies believe will put European companies at an unfair disadvantage on the world stage.
"There's no doubt energy is already more expensive in the EU than other trading blocs," said IFIEC's managing director David Williams in February when details of the draft law started to leak out.

U.S. gas and electricity prices are around 30 percent less than in the EU, says IFIEC. The Federation adds that European industry has already achieved high levels of effieciency and that moves to invest in modern plants in order to maintain Europe's international competitiveness would be hurt by the proposal.
Margot Loudon at Eurogas, which represents European gas groups, has said the tax fails to take into account the relative environmental impact of the energy fuels which the EU intends to tax.

Under the EU proposals the minium levy on unleaded gasoline will be raised to 417 Ecu per 1,000 litres from January 1, 1998 from a current rate of 287 Ecu, while diesel rates would rise to 310 Ecu per 1,000 litres from the current 245 Ecu.
The draft would also set a minium tax of 3.5 Ecu a gigajoule for natural gas used as a motor fuel, while electricity would be taxed at 1 Ecu per megawatt out.
Liquid Petroluem Gas (LPG) would be taxed at 141 Ecu per 1,000 kilograms.

The rates apply to motor fuel in general since the Commission has stated it is looking for reduced rates for fuels used in agriculture and public transport. Reduced rates would also apply for fuel used for heating purposes.

The Commission, mindful of the strong opposition to the proposals since they were first mooted late last year, has tried to soothe fears of a pan-European hike in taxes and costs, particuarly at forecourt pumps.

In most cases the actual rates in the EU's 15 states are already above the proposed new minimum levels. The Commission said in a statement earlier this week that the new diesel rates would represent an increse of 11 percent at the pump in Greece, nine percent in Luxembourg and seven percent in both Spain and Portugal.
In the case of unleaded petrol the rise would affect even fewer countries.
